bull.b: PepGen's proprietary Enhanced Delivery Oligonucleotide (EDO) platform addresses a durable, structural barrier in oligonucleotide therapeutics: tissue delivery (including muscle). A platform that meaningfully improves delivery can provide sustained competitive advantage across multiple neuromuscular indications and support scalable pipeline expansion beyond a single program.

Emerging safety and efficacy signals plus regulatory designations in major jurisdictions reduce development and regulatory risk on a structural level. Global enrollment and expected higher-dose cohorts between 2026–2027 imply a persistent development pathway, improving the odds of accelerated review, partnering, or conditional approvals that materially alter long-term commercial prospects.

A low debt-to-equity ratio and meaningful recorded equity reduce near-term refinancing pressure and bankruptcy risk versus highly leveraged peers. This conservative capital structure gives management more strategic optionality (partnering, staged spend) and more runway to advance programs before reliance on costly debt financing becomes necessary.

bear.b: As a development-stage biotech with no product revenue, PepGen lacks internally generated, recurring cash flow to fund operations. This structural reliance on external capital increases execution risk, reduces margin visibility, and makes long-term sustainability contingent on successful trials, partnerships, or repeat financings rather than business-generated cash.

Consistently large negative operating and free cash flow (~-$77M TTM) represents a durable drain on resources. High burn necessitates recurring capital raises or partner funding; over multiple quarters this depletes shareholder equity, forces dilution, and limits ability to self-fund later-stage trials or commercial launch preparations without material external support.

bear.t: Erosion of equity and dilution risk
bear.b: The steady decline in equity signals persistent losses being financed by capital markets. Structurally, repeated dilution to cover development costs can erode existing shareholders' stakes, constrain management's freedom to pursue costly trials, and raise the hurdle for accretive partnerships or M&A absent demonstrable clinical de-risking.
